name: Agent controls platform builder (the owner)
oneLine: 0xVitalii, founder of merces.ai, builds the controls platform for agentic transactions: a Risk Check, a registry of real agents, monitoring and policy enforcement across protocols.
goals: Build a registry of real agents at merces.ai, verified against on-chain identity (ERC-8004), payment history (x402, MPP) and card-network registrations, that separates working agents from placeholders.
Run a Risk Check on an agent before a counterparty pays it, calls its tool or grants it a mandate.
Monitor agent transactions across ERC-8004, x402, MCP paid tools, stablecoin settlement, ERC-3643, ACP, TAP, MPP, Agent Pay, AP2 and UCP from one place.
Enforce policy (spend caps, allowed payees, allowed merchants, pause and revoke) as an independent layer where the protocol has no native hook.
Give merchants, facilitators and wallets a trust signal they can read in one API call.
Keep every claim about an agent sourced and dated so the registry can be audited.
pains: Most ERC-8004 registrations are placeholders and most feedback is Sybil, so the raw registries cannot be used as a trust source without heavy filtering.
Each protocol exposes a different slice of the transaction: x402 shows settlement on chain, ACP and UCP are private REST calls, TAP leaves only edge logs, and AP2 mandates sit inside credentials.
No protocol defines mandate revocation or an emergency pause, so the controls layer has to act through facilitators, wallets or merchants instead of the protocol itself.
Agents spread across 30 chains and several card programs, and their identifiers (agentId, keyid, agent registration) do not map to each other.
Metrics from explorers and leaderboards are inflated, and telling real demand from farming is unsolved.
Vendor specs change monthly, so monitors break when field names change (endpoints to services, score to value).
decisions: Which signals go into the Risk Check and how to weight on-chain feedback, payment history, registrations and attestations.
Where to insert controls: a facilitator plug-in, a wallet policy, a merchant middleware, or an edge verifier.
Which protocols get first-class data coverage, and in what order.
How to score an agent when evidence is thin, and how to show uncertainty.
What to publish openly and what to keep as the platform's own data.
